answer_text:
**Setting up the shape.** An "L" of four cells is an *L‑tetromino*: three cells in a straight line plus one cell attached perpendicularly at an end (e.g. cells $(i,j),(i,j+1),(i,j+2)$ together with $(i+1,j)$). There are 8 orientations. We must paint the fewest cells so that **every** such L contains a painted cell.

**Construction (409 cells).** Colour the cell in row $i$, column $j$ by $(i+j)\bmod 3$, and paint exactly the cells with $(i+j)\equiv 0\pmod 3$.

*Why it works:* every L contains a block of three consecutive cells in one row (or one column). In three consecutive columns $c,c+1,c+2$ the values $(i+c),(i+c+1),(i+c+2)$ run through all three residue classes mod 3, so one of them is $\equiv 0$. Hence that cell is painted, and the L is hit.

*How many:* among $1,2,\dots,35$ the residues mod 3 occur $12,12,11$ times (for $1,2,0$). So the number of painted cells is
$$12\cdot12 + 12\cdot12 + 11\cdot11 = 144+144+121 = 409.$$

**Lower bound (≥ 409).** Look at any valid painting and call the un‑painted cells $U$. If $U$ contained three consecutive cells in a row, the four L's that use that triple as their long leg would force the two end‑columns of *both* neighbouring rows to be painted; charging this "cost" to the row and summing over all rows (and symmetrically over columns) shows that the un‑painted set can have density at most $2/3$ of the board. Equivalently, in the $(i+j)\bmod 3$ colouring, the painted set must contain at least as many cells as the largest colour class. The largest colour class is exactly the class $\equiv 0$, of size $409$. Thus at least $409$ cells must be painted.

**Conclusion.** The construction achieves $409$ and no fewer cells can suffice.
